Subscriber: OUP-Reference Gratis Access; date: 16 May 2018Abstract and Keywords This article offers a retrospective and prospective analysis of the role of cognitive strategies in students’ academic development over the past 25 years

The focus is on those processes that individuals employ to advance their own learning and understanding (learning strategies) and, to a lesser degree, those procedures applied to regulate and monitor that learning and understanding (metacognitive or self-regulatory strategies)
Drawing on a groundbreaking review from 1988, the article examines how students’ epistemic beliefs—their beliefs about knowing and knowledge—may affect strategic engagement
It also considers students’ motivations or emotions that accompany learning and academic development and, therefore, strategic processing
Finally, it describes strategies associated with online learning, the barriers to being strategic in classrooms, and situations in which teachers and students can foster strategic thinking

Keywords: cognitive strategies , academic development , learning strategies , metacognitive strategies , skills , epistemic beliefs , motivations , emotions , online learning , strategic thinking In 1988, Alexander and Judy published a groundbreaking review that sought to bring together two long-established but distinct bodies of theory and research in cognitive psychology, specifically, the literatures on knowledge and strategic processing

As the authors stated at the outset of that critical analysis, there were two undeniable “truisms” about human learning and development that had long existed separately within the educational psychology literature, despite their seemingly symbiotic, if untapped, natures

The first truism was that learners’ knowledge matters to subsequent learning and performance (e.g., Chi, 1985 ; Glaser, 1984 ), and the second was that those learners A Retrospective and Prospective Examination of Cognitive Strategies and Academic Development: Where Have We Come in Twenty-Five Years

It was Alexander and Judy’s contention that these two aforementioned “truths” about student learning and academic development could not be fully understood in isolation
Rather, any attempt to more fully explicate one of these truths demanded understanding of the other
Therefore, these authors set out to bring the research on knowledge and strategic processing into juxtaposition by deriving evidenced-based hypotheses about their interplay
They also set out to articulate an agenda for future research pertaining to the interaction of knowledge and strategies in students’ academic development

In framing the current examination of cognitive-based learning strategies, we have chosen to return to Alexander and Judy’s (1988) often-cited review and interrogate its evidence-based hypotheses and recommendations for future research with two particular purposes in mind

First, retrospectively, we ask whether the issues and concerns outlined in that systematic review endure after more than 25 years of ensuing research, or whether, to the contrary, there has been noticeable progress in the area of cognitive- based learning strategies over the past quarter century
Second, prospectively, we look ahead to what the next 25 years may hold for strategy research and for those invested in student learning and development
In effect, are the recommendations for future research offered by Alexander and Judy in 1988 still pertinent or are there new avenues for inquiry that need to be explored
Certainly, for a chapter devoted to cognitive strategies and academic development, we should legitimately begin with a clear explication of what we personally hold cognitive strategies to be
Thus, let us state from the outset that our focus in this discussion is on the mental or cognitive processes that individuals employ when they engage in problem- solving tasks

While there are various types and classes of cognitive strategies that can be addressed (and that we overview in a subsequent section of this chapter), our particular interest is on those processes that individuals employ to advance their own learning and understanding ( Alexander, Schallert, & Hare, 1991 ; Weinstein & Mayer, 1986 ) and, to a lesser degree, those procedures applied to regulate and monitor that learning and understanding ( Boekaerts, Pintrich, & Zeidner, 2000 )

The former are often referred to as learning strategies ( Weinstein, Goetz, & Alexander, 1988 ), whereas the latter typically fall under the rubric of metacognitive or self-regulatory strategies ( Zimmerman & Schunk, 2011 )
As a consequence of this focus, we thereby preclude any consideration of instructional or pedagogical strategies from this examination

Instructional or pedagogical strategies are those procedures that educators employ to orchestrate a learning environment, influence students’ behaviors or direct their attention, or promote learners’ thinking or strategic

Further, we refrain from any direct consideration of procedures that individuals may intentionally evoke to regulate their behaviors, motivations, or emotions (e.g., Beauregard, Lévesque, & Bourgouin, 2001 ) unless those procedures also involve learning and development in academic domains or in the context of schooling (e.g., Pekrun, Goetz, Titz, & Perry, 2002 )
In both these cases of exclusion, we do not question the importance or merits of such strategic endeavors or the research they represent
We simply cannot do justice to these areas as part of this exploration

Regarding a more detailed characterization of strategies, we direct attention to the definitions of strategies and strategic processing that framed the Alexander and Judy (1988) review—definitions that have guided our empirical investigations over the ensuing decades (e.g., Alexander & Kulikowich, 1991 ; Alexander, Sperl, Buehl, Fives, & Chiu, 2004 ; Murphy & Alexander, 2002 )
Specifically, Alexander and Judy depicted strategies as a “special form of procedural knowledge that can exist in varying degrees of generality or separation” (1988,p
The authors went on to state that strategies are “goal directed procedures that are planfully or intentionally evoked” and “aid in the regulation, execution, or evaluation” of a problem or task (p

Such a conceptualization mirrored definitions of cognitive strategies forwarded by scholars contributing to that expanding literature in the 1970s and 1980s (e.g., Campione & Brown, 1978 ; Weinstein & Mayer, 1986 )

Interestingly, while Alexander and Judy (1988) expressed concern about the clarity with which the terms domains and domain knowledge were conceptualized in the existing empirical literature of the time, they seemingly operated under the assumption that the definition of strategies they proffered was rather noncontroversial

This may have been an unwarranted assumption on the authors’ part, given the conceptual quandary that has since come to light within contemporary research and instructional practice ( Afflerbach, Pearson, & Paris, 2008 ), namely, the differentiation between skills and strategies
Conceptual Quandary: The Boundaries Between Skills and Strategies The distinction between strategies and skills has seemingly blurred over time—a concern strongly expressed by Alexander et al
(1998) and others ( Afflerbach et al., 2008 ; Alexander, 2006 )

(1998) lamented 10 years after the Alexander and Judy (1988) review: Despite the value that practitioners and the public, at large, seemingly place on basic skills or “skillful” behavior, efforts to juxtapose conceptions of strategic and skillful performance have been relatively rare in the literature

It is one thing to acknowledge that a quandary exists between conceptions of strategies and skills in human learning and academic development that mark educational discourse
It is quite another to understand why they exist or how to address such problems

Of course, some of the more obvious but simplistic explanations for this continuing conceptual problem can be laid at the feet of educational researchers and practitioners who are careless in the language they use or negligent in providing explicit definitions of terms they employ ( Alexander et al., 1991 ; Murphy & Alexander, 2000 )
However, there are more complex and problematic reasons that must be forwarded

For one, this conceptual problem may, in part, be a side effect of the regularity with which students’ strategic abilities and strategic processing are touted within educational policies ( Common Core State Standards Initiative [CCSS], 2010 ) or instructional practice (Afflerbach & Cho, 2008 , 2010 )—a promotion that too often occurs in the absence of explicit definitions of key terms ( Alexander et al., 1991 ; Murphy & Alexander, 2000 )
As a result, the more the term strategies has come to populate the educational discourse, the less its meaning vis-à-vis skills has been effectively communicated or embodied (Alexander et al., 1998 )
This lack of clarity is more than a semantic dilemma, but comes with serious instructional and assessment consequences, as Afflerbach et al

Another contributor to the fact that the terms strategies and skills are often used interchangeably in the literature ( Alexander et al., 1998 ) may be that these two critical forms of process do share certain attributes
For instance, both represent forms of procedural knowledge essential for human learning and academic performance that must be acquired and honed over time
Nonetheless, there are significant differences between strategies and skills that should not be ignored
(1998) noted: These differences pertain to the automaticity of performance and to learner awareness or intentionality
That is, students hone these techniques to a level of automaticity, enabling them to perform a given task fluidly and effectively
Skills are the “habits” of performance, or what a learner typically does ( James, 1890 )
… When students’ routine techniques or typical approaches are not enough to resolve a given situation, conscious, intentional, and effortful processing must take over
… When this conscious, intentional, and effortful processing takes over, the learner is performing strategically

135) Surprisingly, when we fast forward 20 years since Alexander and Judy’s (1988) article, we find that this confounding of skills and strategies remains problematic, as evidenced by the arguments articulated by Afflerbach et al

Such inconsistency can confuse students and teachers and render instruction less effective

(2008) sought to resolve the confusion they identified in the reading literature by establishing that it is important that the terms skill and strategy be used to distinguish automatic processes from deliberately controlled processes
371) But, this seeming failure to recognize the conscious, intentional, and effortful character of strategies is not solely a problem of educational practice

Rather, it is reflected in the empirical research that attempts to investigate learners’ strategic processing but that does not seem to disentangle such “deliberate and controlled processes” ( Afflerbach et al., 2008 ,p
371) from the habituated or automatic processing in which students engage (Campione & Brown, 1978 )

This remains problematic even in studies by researchers (ourselves included) who conceptually acknowledge this critical distinction between skills and strategies but find it challenging, if not impossible, to distinguish automatic or habitual processes applied to some cognitive task from those that have a more conscious and effortful character ( Dinsmore & Alexander, 2012 )

This discrepancy between the conceptualization and operationalization of strategies in much educational research may arise, in part, from the methods commonly employed to unearth cognitive processes during task performance, such as think-alouds ( Pressley & Afflerbach, 1995 )

As has long been argued, such methods, while invaluable for transforming internal or tacit thoughts into external and explicit data, inevitably alter the very processes being investigated ( Ericsson & Simon, 1998 ; Winne & Perry, 2000 )
The consequence of such transformations for the study of cognitive strategies (versus skills) is especially noteworthy
For instance, consider when students are called on to verbalize whatever they are thinking or doing when cognitively engaged

Researchers analyzing such think-aloud data cannot hope to definitively determine whether the voiced processes are evidence of respondents’ “default” or skillful manner of operation or indicative of their more intentional actions

Of course, the degree to which think-alouds or other data- gathering procedures (e.g., retrospective or structured interviews) become intrusive can be carefully addressed in their implementation ( Pressley & Afflerbach, 1995 )

Because of the importance that data-gathering procedures play in the study of cognitive strategies, we revisit this issue of research methodologies when we consider future directions by exploring alternative or complementary research techniques
Yet another contributory factor in this conceptual confusion may have a more pragmatic and pedagogical root
Specifically, as theoretically established, a critical distinction between strategic and skillful processing rests in the degree of automaticity or

Thus, when educators teach procedures for predicting, summarizing, or clarifying, it may not be evident at the time whether they are teaching procedures that will remain intentional and effortful for those students (i.e., strategies) or eventually reach automaticity for them (i.e., skills)
In other words, the ultimate distinction in this case will reside in the way in which these essential procedures are internalized and activated by the learners themselves
Because educators must operate in the dark to some extent, it may be understandable that their use of terms like strategies or skills to denote these cognitive procedures remains obscured
We revisit issues pertaining to the teaching of strategies later in this chapter

Contributions of Epistemic Beliefs and Motivation/Emotion Research Because human intentionality and effortfulness are cast as so pivotal to the aforementioned distinction between strategies and skills, there are emerging bodies of research that would seem to be particularly relevant to this discussion

The first pertains to the beliefs about knowing and knowledge that students hold and the effect that those beliefs may exert on strategic engagement ( Murphy, Alexander, & Muis, 2012 ; Murphy & Mason, 2006 )

For instance, because knowledge is a centerpiece of this partnership, individuals’ beliefs about knowledge and knowing—epistemic beliefs—are naturally entering the landscape in strategy theory and research ( Muis, 2007 ; Sinatra & Pintrich, 2002 )

Thus, it seems reasonable to assume that decisions to engage in conscious, deliberate, and effortful procedures to promote learning and performance would be influenced by students’ beliefs regarding whether knowledge is simple or complex or whether it is bestowed by authorities or derived via critical analysis and justification (Alexander et al., 2011 ; Schommer, 1993 )

The second encompasses students’ motivations or emotions that accompany learning and academic development and, therefore, students’ strategic processing ( Linnenbrink-Garcia & Pekrun, 2011 ; Pekrun et al., 2002 )
Indeed, the research on motivations and emotions represents two of the most fertile lines of inquiry to take form since the publication of the Alexander and Judy article
Acknowledging the significance of these lines of inquiry to the nature of strategic (vs

skillful) processing, the Alexander and Judy wrote: Because strategies, as we have operationally defined them, are characterized by planful and intentional use, [strategies’] susceptibility to motivational effects may be rather considerable
… One recent volume, devoted specifically to the topic of metacognition, motivation, and understanding offers an extended discussion of the relationship between strategy use and motivation
396) Because we cannot help to do justice to these two domains of inquiry, we only briefly acknowledge their roles as contributors to the distinctions between strategies and skills
We leave it to others, including contributors to this volume, to extend this discussion.

Subscriber: OUP-Reference Gratis Access; date: 16 May 2018With this conceptual overview in place, we now turn to other specifics about cognitive strategies and student learning and performance

Specifically, within the retrospective frame, we explore the various types and levels of strategies suggested by Alexander and Judy’s (1988) review, especially with regard to the topics of domain-general versus domain-specific and higher order versus lower order strategies
Through the prospective lens, we then query the literature to identify new manifestations of strategic processing that may merit increased attention in the decades to come
Similarly, reaching back into the literature, we revisit concerns over the failure to foster and facilitate students’ strategic thinking and performance within the context of schools

Then, we peer ahead to consider general and specific steps that can be taken within schools and classrooms to bolster the likelihood of effective strategic processing by students who populate those educational environments

Types of Strategies As noted, Alexander and Judy (1988) identified the lack of clarity within the educational and psychological literature regarding what constitutes a strategy as a substantial roadblock for strategy research
Of particular concern was the impact of this lack of clarity on investigations that examined the relation between strategic processing and domain knowledge

Specifically, Alexander and Judy posited the recommendation that “future investigations should provide clear operational definitions and detailed descriptions of the subjects, domains, and strategies involved” (p

They also argued that the conceptual confusion arising from unclear operational definitions “seems particularly acute when we try to discern the relationship of more domain-specific strategies to those of a more general or executive nature” (p
Given the focus of Alexander and Judy’s 1988 review on the relation between domain knowledge and strategic processing, the question of the domain specificity of strategies was essential
In the 25 years since, the relation between domain knowledge and strategy use has been well established in the empirical literature (e.g., Alexander et al., 1998 ;E
Yet, has the distinction between domain-specific and domain- general strategies been clarified in the intervening years
Moreover, the interplay between strategies and knowledge extends beyond questions of domain generality or specificity to concerns about the depth and level of strategic processing

Thus, we turn our attention to a discussion of three specific classes of strategies that would signify not only a relation between cognitive strategies and knowledge but also academic development more broadly: (a) domain general and domain specific, (b) deep processing and surface processing, and (c) cognitive and metacognitive
Our primary purpose is to interrogate the literature to determine whether we have achieved the greater sense of clarity called for by Alexander and Judy (1988) .

Subscriber: OUP-Reference Gratis Access; date: 16 May 2018However, before we embark on this endeavor, we forward one critical caveat

As with distinctions between and among constructs that populate the educational psychological literature, there are rarely clean or truly dichotomous relations between classes of strategies—regardless of how we choose to categorize them
It may be advantageous to set deep against surface, for instance, or domain general against domain specific to sharpen contrasts between such classes of strategies
But, reality is that there is little justification for any true dichotomization in these instances
The distinctions that may exist are potentially more continuous as opposed to discrete in nature
Further, marked differences in the nature of learners, tasks, or contexts can reposition any specific problem-solving procedure along its defining continuum
Thus, what qualifies as a surface-level strategy for Learner A performing TaskB in ContextC would more accurately qualify as a deep-processing strategy for LearnerX engaged in TaskY within ContextZ

With this in mind, we address the challenge of conceptual clarity, confronting whether and how those types of strategies have been defined and examined within the literature, and whether the “lack of understanding” (p

Domain-General and Domain-Specific Strategies For Alexander and Judy (1988) , the need to understand whether strategies are specific for tasks within a single domain or whether they generalize across domains was critical
They noted: To some, strategies are general processes that operate across domains … whereas to others they are compilations or extensions of domain-specific knowledge

382) Because they found that researchers tended to hold either a domain-general or a domain- specific view of strategies, Alexander and Judy subsequently discussed these classes of strategies as related, highlighting the importance of clarification in order to examine the relation between domain-general and domain-specific strategies

To this end, they pointed to a hierarchical framework for understanding distinctions between domain-general and domain-specific strategies forwarded by Pressley, Goodchild, Fleet, Zajchowski, and Evans (1989)

In this framework, Pressley, Goodchild, and colleagues (1989) identified several main categories of strategies that differ in their ability to generalize across domains (i.e., specific field of study; Muis, Bendixen, & Haerle, 2006 )

These range from strategies that are used to accomplish domain-specific tasks (e.g., mnemonics to remember the lines of a musical staff) to those that can be applied across many domains (e.g., activating prior knowledge)
Domain-general strategies are strategies that can be applied to tasks and problems in a wide variety of content areas

These include cognitive strategies such as rereading, questioning, and idea generation ( Murphy & Alexander, 2002 ; Pressley & Afflerbach, 1995 ; Youssef, Ayers, & Sweller, 2012 ), in addition to metacognitive strategies

Domain-general strategies can be traced back to research in reading, problem-solving, and memorizing, and they tend to rely on heuristics ( Edwards Olshavsky, 1976 ; Flavell, Friedrichs, & Hoyt, 1970 ; Garner, 1982 ; Weir, 1964 )

In contrast, domain-specific strategies are those instantiated in a single domain, for the purpose of engaging in the tasks, activities, and goals specific to the domain at hand ( Pressley, Goodchild, et al., 1989 ; Sweller, 1990 )

Domain-specific strategies are frequently algorithmic ( Case & Marshall, 2004 ) and include common examples such as the five-paragraph sandwich model for essay writing, the FOIL (first, outer, inner, last) method in algebra, and the use of roman numerals to identify chord progressions in music
In the past 25 years, perhaps the most widely researched domain-general strategies are those related to reading (e.g., Afflerbach, 1990 ; Cerdán & Vidal-Abarca, 2008 ; Murphy & Alexander, 2002 )

While certain reading-related strategies are domain specific because they are tied directly to the text (e.g., figuring out the meaning of a word in context, adjusting the rate of reading), many strategies related to reading comprehension are of a more general character

Given the nature of reading as a means for learning in a wide variety of domains ( Alfassi, 2008 ; Shanahan & Shanahan, 2008 ), and given the historical roots of prominent reading researchers in the study of strategic processing (e.g., Garner, 1982 ; Pressley, Johnson, Symons, McGoldrick, & Kurita, 1989 ; van Dijk & Kintsch, 1983 ), it is no surprise that these strategies have been prominently featured in the domain- general strategy literature
As the context in which students engage in reading has shifted monumentally in the past 25 years, so has the focus on reading-related strategies

In this time, research on strategies related to searching for, selecting, and evaluating texts, as well as integrating across multiple texts, has been introduced and has begun to receive greater attention ( Anmarkrud, Bråten, & Strømsø, 2014 ; Kurby, Britt, & Magliano, 2005 ; Wineburg, 1991 )
We return to the discussion of online learning strategies later in this chapter

Whether domain specific or domain general, strategies do not operate without a context, and findings related to the success of domain-general relative to domain-specific strategies are contingent on understanding that context ( Afflerbach & Cho, 2008 )
Yet, is the domain in which strategies are applied made evident in strategy research
Alexander and Judy noted that much of the general strategy research offered “at best, a weak articulation of the content area in which the strategy or strategies were applied” (1988,p
In addition to a lack of identification of domains, they suggested that the domain in which strategies are examined should be purposeful
They argued, “It would also facilitate our understanding of the content-strategy relationship to have some information as to why particular domains were selected for investigation” (1988,p
Such domain considerations are important, given the critical nature of domain differences outlined by Alexander and Judy (1988) and others ( Afflerbach & Cho, 2008 ; Alexander et al., 1998 ).

Subscriber: OUP-Reference Gratis Access; date: 16 May 2018In 25 years, how well has strategy research met this call for clarity
In a 2012 review of deep and surface processing, Dinsmore and Alexander found that approximately 40% of studies did not situate strategic processing within a domain

This is not surprising given the directions of many strategy questionnaires, such as the Motivated Strategies for Learning Questionnaire (MSLQ; Pintrich, Smith, Garcia, & McKeachie, 1993 ) and the inventory of learning processes (ILP; Schmeck, Ribich, & Ramanaiah, 1977 ) to report general dispositions toward strategic processing
Samuelstuen and Bråten (2007) argued that such self-report global strategy measures have limited validity evidence

In this argument, they identified challenges both to students’ ability to provide accurate judgments regarding their strategy use and limited criterion validity between global strategy measures and performance on academic tasks
As such, they suggested that adapting measures to focus responses on task-specific instances provides a more accurate measure of strategy use and serves as a better predictor for task performance
Breaking domain-specific strategies into task-specific strategies provides a more specific context for the consideration of strategic processing ( Hagan, Braasch, & Bråten, 2014 )
Samuelstuen and Bråten’s (2007) position harkens back to Pressley, Johnson, et al
(1989) conceptualization of domain-specific strategies as strategies limited to applications in a limited number of tasks within a domain

Since the publication of Alexander and Judy’s 1988 review, the importance of understanding the role of domain-specific versus domain-general strategies within a given context has been noted by a few studies that specifically addressed such issues (Pokay & Blumenfeld, 1990 )

For instance, in a study of students in a high school geometry course, Pokay and Blumenfeld (1990) found that reported use of domain- specific and domain-general strategies was related; however, strategies specific to geometry predicted achievement in the course, but general strategies did not
This is not to suggest that domain-general strategies do not support learning

Consistent with the second truism presented in Alexander and Judy’s 1988 examination of strategic processing and domain knowledge, it has been well documented that students who use domain-general strategies have increased learning (e.g., Chinnappin & Lawson, 1996 ; Pape & Wang, 2003 ; Youssef et al., 2012 )
Moreover, the goals of education to support higher order or critical thinking suggest that domain-general strategies should be the standard for developing students as strategic individuals

For students, the ability to apply strategies across a number of situations and domains not only is more efficient than learning domain-specific or task-specific strategies, but also is a hallmark of higher order thinking ( Alexander et al., 2011 ; Resnick, 1987 )

Given concerns with measurement of domain-general strategies (Samuelstuen & Bråten, 2007 ) and the need to situate studies of strategic processing within carefully selected domains ( Alexander & Judy, 1988 ), research examining the application of general cognitive strategies across tasks and domains will be necessary for understanding the degree to which these strategies relate to academic performance and to more accurately assess their relation to domain-specific strategies.

Subscriber: OUP-Reference Gratis Access; date: 16 May 2018Deep-Processing and Surface-Processing Strategies In addition to the division of strategies as domain specific or domain general, for the past 40 years, the educational psychology literature has also distinguished strategies in terms of the depth of processing that strategies entail (Marton & Säljö, 1976a , 1976b )
The presence of this distinction has increased in empirical research since that time ( Dinsmore & Alexander, 2012 )
Surface-processing strategies are defined as strategies used to make sense of the problem at hand ( Dinsmore & Alexander, 2012 ; Nolen, 1988 )
In contrast, deep-processing strategies are used to integrate, transform, or evaluate a problem (Alexander et al., 2005; Nolen & Haladyna, 1990 )

Surface-processing strategies include rereading, underlining, and rehearsing points to remember ( Phan, 2009 ; Pressley & Afflerbach, 1995 ; Rodriguez, 2009 ), while deep-processing strategies include elaborating on main ideas, identifying an underlying argument, and providing justification for a claim (Alexander, 2003 ; Chin & Brown, 2000 ; Nolen, 1988 ; Pressley & Afflerbach, 1995 )
One of the first models to differentiate levels of strategic processing was the approaches to learning model developed by Marton and Säljö ( 1976a , 1976b ) and modified by Biggs (1987)
In their model, Marton and Säljö (1976a) regarded deep processing and surface processing as approaches to learning that vary across individuals (1976a) and across tasks (1976b)

Through a series of studies, they suggested that some individuals are more likely to solve problems using deep-processing strategies, while others might be more inclined to use surface-processing strategies ( Marton & Säljö, 1976a )

Additionally, although noting that the type of questions that are asked elicit differences in strategies, they maintained their focus on strategic processing as a style of learning that differs across individuals, indicating that certain types of questions result in a deep-processing approach while others result in a surface-processing approach

Marton and Säljö’s (1976a , 1976b ) conceptualization was based on reading research with undergraduates, and as such, in their model, surface processing was concerned with strategies related to the replication of text, while deep processing was concerned with strategies for understanding the main ideas and principles of text
Along a similar framework to Marton and Säljö ( 1976a , 1976b ), Biggs (1987) identified three levels of processing approaches, focusing on undergraduates’ study habits
His levels ranged from the most surface-level processing (i.e., reproducing), to a moderate level (i.e., internalizing), and one consistent with deep-level processing (i.e., organizing)

In contrast to the approaches of learning model, information-processing models have used levels of processing to explain the encoding and storage of memories ( Craik & Lockhart, 1972 ; Craik & Tulving, 1975 ; Kapur et al., 1994 )
The information-processing framework describes memories as moving from sensory to short-term to long-term storage ( Baddeley, 1992 )

During this process, levels of processing are used to explain the degree of analysis individuals exercise to make sense of sensory input and information stored in short-term and long-term memory ( Craik & Lockhart, 1972 )
In this model, surface-processing strategies include rehearsing information, while deep-processing strategies include elaboration and connection to prior knowledge ( Craik & Tulving, 1975 ).

Subscriber: OUP-Reference Gratis Access; date: 16 May 2018The level of processing is regarded as varying according to the meaningfulness of the information presented, level of attention paid, and degree of overlap with current cognitive schemas ( Craik & Lockhart, 1972 )
Accordingly, deep-processing strategies would most likely occur if the information is presented meaningfully, carefully attended, and aligns closely with an individual’s existing schemas

Similar to the approaches to learning model, deep-processing strategies in the information-processing approach are associated with more efficient and effective retention of memory than surface-processing strategies

Building on earlier models that differentiated deep and surface processing, Alexander created the Model of Domain Learning (MDL; Alexander, 1997 , 2003 ), which situated deep and surface processing within the changes that occur across academic development and described developmental trajectories of deep- and surface-processing strategies

Unlike the approaches to learning model, the MDL provides for the concurrent use of surface- and deep-processing strategies within an individual and focuses on the interrelated changes in knowledge, motivation, and strategic processing that occur across development

In her MDL, Alexander ( 1997 , 2003 ) suggested that as individuals move from the earliest stages of development within a domain (i.e., acclimation) to the more advanced stages of competence and proficiency, they tend to rely less on surface- processing strategies and more on deep-processing strategies
In 1988, Alexander and Judy noted that “as knowledge in a domain increases, strategic processing is altered” (p
They discussed differences between novices and experts, alluding to differences in surface-processing and deep-processing strategy use between these groups

While in 1988 there was a tendency to believe that deep strategies are better than surface, Alexander and Judy (1988) indicated that the level of strategic processing required to complete a task may necessarily depend on the characteristics of the learner
The MDL built on research on expertise, allowing for a continuum of development and taking into account the differences in domain knowledge that were central to Alexander and Judy (1988) ’s review
In the past decades, certain misconceptions about deep- and surface-level strategic processing have emerged in the literature, misconceptions that present challenges to the task of reaching clarity

First, deep- and surface-processing strategies have been bifurcated, often with the belief that deep-processing strategies are always better than surface-processing strategies ( Beattle, Collins, & McInnes, 1997 ; Dinsmore & Alexander, 2012 )
Similar challenges to the view of higher levels of processing as superior to lower levels have been brought forward with regard to higher order and lower order thinking (Alexander et al., 2011 )

However, despite the common belief by both researchers and students that deep-processing strategies are better for learning than surface-processing strategies ( Nolen, 1988 ), empirical research has provided inconsistent findings ( Block, 2009 ; Cano, 2007 )
Dinsmore and Alexander (2012) credited this inconsistency to a lack of consideration for the context of learning
Moreover, the interaction of individual factors with strategic processing suggests that deep-processing strategies should not be expected and may not

Just as Alexander and Judy (1988) thoroughly examined the interaction between strategies and domain knowledge, it will be important for research moving forward to examine the interaction between levels of processing and the contexts and situations in which deep, surface, or a combination of strategies best support learning

The second misconception is that deep-processing and surface-processing strategies are frequently perceived as orientations to learning ( Entwhistle, 1991 ; Marton & Säljö, 1976a ) rather than part of a repertoire of strategies that individuals can apply across varied contexts and domains
In this sense, individuals are considered to be deep processors or surface processors (e.g., Verheij, Stoutjesdijk, & Beishuizen, 1996 )

Perceiving strategy use as an approach to learning is consistent with Marton and Säljö’s (1976a) initial conceptualization; however, as they and others later identified ( Marton & Säljö, 1976b ; Ramsden, 1997 ), the task in which individuals engage can alter whether deep-processing or surface-processing strategies are most advantageous

Empirical research has found that individuals tend to use both deep-processing and surface- processing strategies during tasks such as reading ( Pressley & Afflerbach, 1995 ; Afflerbach & VanSledright, 2001 ; Hagan et al., 2014 ) and learning ( Aharony, 2006 ; Dunlosky, Rawson, Marsh, Nathan, & Willingham, 2013 )

Additionally, models such as the MDL have suggested that while individuals may have a propensity to use particular levels of strategies depending on their stage of academic development within a domain, these strategies work in conjunction and vary according to the domain in which individuals engage
Returning to Alexander and Judy’s (1988) call for strategies to be clearly defined, it is important to consider whether research on surface-processing and deep-processing strategies has met this goal

A recent review of deep- and surface-processing strategies by Dinsmore and Alexander (2012) identified this as still problematic and implicated it as a problem that seems to be growing as interest in research on levels of strategic processing has become more frequent since the 1980s
In their systematic review, Dinsmore and Alexander (2012) noted changes in the occurrence of definitions of deep- and surface-processing strategies over time

While definitions were provided for all but one article prior to 2000, a substantial proportion of articles published after 2000 did not include explicit definitions, a finding they suggested may be due to the increased prevalence of research in this area leading researchers to believe that definitions may not be necessary

However, as Alexander and Judy (1988) noted and as was evident in our previous discussion of strategies versus skills, the increase in research does not indicate that definitions should be discarded, rather that clarity should become more important as separate lines of inquiry are brought together

Subscriber: OUP-Reference Gratis Access; date: 16 May 2018Despite the specific focus of this chapter on cognitive learning strategies, we find it essential to recognize an additional class of strategies that are frequently considered in tandem with cognitive strategies: metacognitive strategies
In 1987, Ruth Garner devoted space in her book on Metacognition and Reading Comprehension to explaining the somewhat confusing association between cognitive and metacognitive strategies

The deceptively simple differentiation she offered was the enactment of mental procedures to rectify or enhance performance (cognitive strategies), the oversight or monitoring of those procedures (metacognitive strategies), or the overarching knowledge and experiences individuals have about their strategic capabilities (metacognitive knowledge and metacognitive experiences)

In his seminal writings on metacognition, Flavell (1979) also acknowledged the challenge of separating cognitive and metacognitive strategies, acknowledging that the same strategy could be used to meet the cognitive goals of rectifying or enhancing performance as well as the metacognitive goals of overseeing or monitoring that performance

Metacognitive strategies are frequently regarded as guiding individuals’ decisions about their use and implementation of cognitive strategies ( Flavell, 1979 ; Pressley, Johnson, et al., 1989 ; Purpura, 1997 ; Vrugt & Oort, 2008 )

As such, metacognitive strategies are intertwined with cognitive strategies, and the reciprocal process between metacognition and cognition presents a challenge for defining and measuring the strategies separately (Veenman, Van-Hout Wolters, & Afflerbach, 2006 )

Nonetheless, in recent studies, cognitive and metacognitive strategy use have been found to be distinct, yet positively related, to performance for tasks such as visuospatial construction ( Dermitzaki, Leondari, & Goudas, 2009 ); reading comprehension ( Yang, 2012 ); and second-language learning (Hsiao & Oxford, 2002 )

Moreover, as the interplay between domain knowledge and cognitive strategic processing has been established ( Alexander et al., 1998 ; Alexander & Judy, 1988 ; Harris, Alexander, & Graham, 2008 ), so has the relation between metacognitive strategies and knowledge, especially in the expanding literature on experts and expertise development ( Schraw, 1998 )

In brief, those who demonstrate greater expertise in a given domain or with particular problem-solving tasks likewise display greater metacognitive knowledge and strategic behavior over those who are less expert (Alexander et al., 2004 ; Ericsson, Krampe, & Tesch-Römer, 1993 )

Over the past quarter century, there has been much less attention paid to the cognitive versus metacognitive distinction and much more dialogue directed to the relation between metacognitive and self-regulatory strategies, which both involve monitoring or regulation ( Azevedo, 2009 ;E

Given the growing presence of theory and research on self-regulation over the past 25 years (Schunk, 2008 ; Zimmerman, 1995 , 2002 ), this debate over what constitutes metacognitive versus self-regulatory strategies shows no signs of abating ( Dinsmore, Alexander, & Loughlin, 2008 )
However, it is beyond the scope and intention of this chapter to seek to tease apart the complex relation between metacognitive and self-regulatory strategies.

Mason & Ariasi, 2011 ; Moeller, Klein, & Nuerk, 2011 ), with some work in neurophysiological methods (e.g., Cho, Ryali, Geary, & Menon, 2011 ; Grabner et al., 2009 )
With the exception of neurophysiological methods, the other types of measures were present a quarter century ago

However, the years since have brought about certain transformations in the popularity of particular measures as well as advances in technology, which have aided the ability of researchers to collect real-time measures of strategic processing.

Common strategy self-report questionnaires include the MSLQ ( Pintrich et al., 1993 ); the Study Process Questionnaire (SPQ; Biggs, 1987 ); and the ILP ( Schmeck et al., 1977 )

These questionnaire measures direct individuals to report their typical manner of processing, aligning more closely to theoretical models by Marton and Säljö (1976a) and Biggs (1987) and focusing on domain-general strategies

While these measures have a long history of use in educational research with established psychometric properties (Pintrich & De Groot, 1990 ; Pintrich et al., 1993 ; Schmeck et al., 1977 ) and have been found to relate to academic performance ( Eshel & Kohavi, 2003 ; Vrugt & Oort, 2008 ), they present challenges for researchers examining strategy use as a flexible, goal- directed process that varies across tasks and contexts

Some researcher-developed questionnaire measures have addressed this issue of task and context specificity ( Bråten & Strømsø, 2011 ; Schellings, 2011 ), and others have applied more general measures to various contexts ( Wolters & Pintrich, 1998 )
Participants completing these measures are directed to provide either prospective or retrospective reports related to a specific task
Prospective strategy measures, completed prior to engaging in a task, instruct individuals to identify the strategies that they plan to use while completing the task (e.g., Cromley & Azevedo, 2006 )

In contrast, retrospective strategy measures occur following a task and instruct participants to report the strategies that they implemented during the given task (Bråten & Strømsø, 2011 ; Murphy & Alexander, 2002 )

The assignment of strategy conditions in experimental research is a methodology used when task variations are believed to elicit different types of strategic processing (e.g., Grodsky & Giambra, 1990 ; Freed, Marshall, & Phillips, 1998 ) or when individuals are taught different strategies (or no strategies) depending on their condition (e.g.,L.H
Conditions that differ according to task variations are frequently associated with studies examining differences in deep- and surface-processing strategies ( Dinsmore & Alexander, 2012 )

For instance, in a study on reading comprehension strategies, students were instructed when to use the specific strategies of rereading, paraphrasing, and self-explaining ( Moss, Schunn, Schneider, McNamara, & VanLehn, 2011 )
These different types of strategies were verified in terms of self-reported use and then correlated with regions of brain activation

Strategy intervention research often follows the method of assigning some groups of individuals to receive instruction of the use and implementation of certain strategies, while other individuals serve as a control (e.g., Graham, Harris, & Mason, 2005 )
In these conditions, strategies are frequently taught one at a time or as small clusters of strategies ( Spörer et al., 2009 )

These methods originated in expert/ novice and problem-solving research (e.g., Ericsson & Simon, 1980 ; Simon & Chase, 1973 ) and later expanded to reading ( Pressley & Afflerbach, 1995 )

Unlike the questionnaire measures, think-aloud methods provide a measure of real-time processing, asking participants to talk aloud and report what they are doing as they are completing a task or solving a problem
Processes are then coded according to the types and specific strategies reported
Amid concerns that thinking aloud during a task such as reading changes the process or that individuals are not able to accurately report the strategies they employ ( Dunlosky & Hertzog, 2001 ;M.C
Fox, Ericsson, & Best, 2011 ; Pressley & Afflerbach, 1995 ), these methodologies continue to be frequently used within the strategic-processing literature ( Afflerbach, 2000 ;E
Eye tracking provides a complementary of real-time processing ( Just & Carpenter, 1980 ) through the examination of eye movements (i.e., saccades)
It is used both independently and concurrently with other measures such as think-alouds and questionnaires ( Kaakinen & Hyönä, 2005 )

As a measure of strategy use, eye-tracking measures have followed a similar historical trajectory as think-alouds, emanating in research on expertise and problem-solving ( Abernethy & Russell, 1987 ; Just & Carpenter, 1976 ) and later implemented for use in studies of reading ( Just & Carpenter, 1980 ; Rayner, 1978 )

As a measure of strategic processing, eye tracking provides data about the time spent on specific visual elements, such as the time spent on answer choices to a multiple-choice problem relative to the time spent on the stem ( Vakil, Lifshitz, Tzuriel, Weiss, & Arzuoan, 2011 ; Vigneau, Caissie, & Bors, 2006 )

During reading tasks, eye tracking provides information about the time spent on individual words, the number of look backs to specific words, and the relative time spent on text compared to other visual elements such as graphs ( Ariasi & Mason, 2011 ; Hannus & Hyönä, 1999 ; Hyönä, Lorch, & Kaakinen, 2002 )

From these data, researchers make inferences about the use of processes such as rereading, understanding a word in context, and the identification of anomalous words ( Rayner, Chance, Slatterby, & Ashby, 2006 )

Although eye tracking has existed for more than a century ( Rayner, 1998 ) and was available when Alexander and Judy (1988) published their review, it has been more prominent in strategy research over the past several decades ( Rayner, 1998 )
In contrast, the use of neuroscientific methodologies in strategic-processing research was virtually nonexistent 25 years ago

While neurophysiological methods have remained limited in both their frequency of use and the degree to which they can capture real-time strategic processing, they have received increasing interest in recent years (e.g., Grabner & De Smedt, 2012 ; Newman, Willoughby, & Price, 2011 )
At the current time, most technologies associated with neurophysiological investigations of strategy use present important advantages and disadvantages

For example, functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) machines collect information about the location and sequence of a participant’s brain activation while doing a task— allowing for an unprecedented view of cognition—but, at the same time, limit the types of

In comparison, methods such as functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) and event- related potentials (ERPs) allow a participant to move his or her head and to speak during an experiment, which provides for a much wider range of tasks to be used but comes with their own specific limitations

For example, participants can think aloud or interact with one another while an fNIRS machine records the activation in their cerebral cortex (Dresler et al., 2009 ; Hatta et al., 2009 ), but activation in other, further-from-the-skull brain regions cannot be detected

Expanding Classes of Strategies In the years since the publication of Alexander and Judy’s (1988) review, much has been learned about the characterization of strategies and strategy use
But, in these intervening years, has the field come to identify new classes or types of strategies that warrant further examination
That is to say, has the field grown not only in the relative depth of what is known, but also in the breadth of strategic processes that are under investigation

In this section, we offer two principal areas of study in which empirical research and accompanying scholarly debate have gained prominence in recent years and in which, in our estimation, scholarly interest is likely to continue to grow: (a) metastrategies and (b) strategies for online learning

We turn to a critical examination of each of these areas of study, explicating these types of strategies and whether they are in fact “new” types of strategies or iterations of previous conceptualizations

Subscriber: OUP-Reference Gratis Access; date: 16 May 2018Metastrategies are strategies that learners employ to regulate or monitor their learning, understanding, and strategy use

In this way, some of the types of strategies previously described in this chapter, like metacognitive strategies (e.g., Pintrich, 1991 ) and self- regulatory strategies (e.g., Schunk, 2008 ), can be considered members of the class of metastrategies
The key difference between metastrategies and other cognitive learning strategies is that metastrategies are used to guide or monitor an individual’s use of more specific cognitive strategies
This guiding or monitoring of cognitive strategies by metastrategies can occur across a variety of domains
In a sense, metastrategies are always domain general, although it is likely that individuals are not as adept in applying these strategies in all domains ( Schraw, 1998 ; Veenman et al., 2006 )
Whenever a learner is strategically regulating personal strategy use, the learner can be said to be employing a metastrategy

While descriptions of metastrategies themselves (i.e., metacognitive and self-regulatory strategies) have existed in the educational and psychological literature for some time (e.g., Flavell, 1981 ; Garner, 1987 ), recent years have seen the class of metastrategies broadened in significant ways
Specifically, the characterization of relational reasoning strategies as metastrategies has opened new opportunities for the study of metastrategies and the academic outcomes to which they are linked
These relational reasoning metastrategies, their utility to learners, and their associated research traditions are now discussed

Relational reasoning metastrategies are cognitive procedures purposely applied to recognizing or deriving meaningful relations or patterns between and among pieces of information that may otherwise appear unrelated ( Alexander & the Disciplined Reading and Learning Research Lab [DRLRL], 2012 )

The ability to employ these strategies is regarded as fundamental to human cognitive function ( Hofstadter, 2001 ; James, 1890 ; Sternberg, 1977 ) and education (e.g., Richland, Zur, & Holyoak, 2007 )
It has been identified as an important ability associated with early learning ( Goswami, 1992 ), as well as a hallmark of expertise, especially in scientific domains ( Dunbar, 1995 )

Relational reasoning strategies require students to engage in deeper level processing of information than they may otherwise do ( Holyoak, 2012 ) and may counteract the tendency of students to treat information in an isolated or piecemeal way ( Braasch & Goldman 2010 )

While the bulk of the literature on relational reasoning characterizes the construct as an ability or trait and not as a body of strategies available for students to learn and employ (Krawczyk, 2012 ), a growing body of work puts strategic processing at the forefront of conceptualizations of relational reasoning (e.g., Alexander & the DRLRL, 2012 ; Alexander, Dumas, Grossnickle, List, & Firetto, 2016 ; Richland & McDonough, 2010 )

This characterization of relational reasoning as a body of metastrategies to be employed has potential to be informative for programs of research that focus on both relational reasoning specifically and metastrategies in general.

Subscriber: OUP-Reference Gratis Access; date: 16 May 2018Here, we briefly discuss four particular relational reasoning metastrategies that have been put forward as warranting further systematic investigation (e.g., Alexander & Baggetta, 2014 ; Alexander et al., 2016
These four metastrategies have been extensively reviewed elsewhere ( Alexander & the DRLRL, 2012 ; Dumas, Alexander, & Grossnickle, 2013 )
The four relational reasoning metastrategies considered in this chapter are analogy, anomaly, antinomy, and antithesis
An analogic strategy is a procedure purposely applied to the identification of a relational similarity between two or more concepts, objects, or situations ( Bostrom, 2008 ; Hesse, 1959 )

The ability to employ analogical reasoning strategies has been shown to be instrumental in knowledge transfer ( Gentner, Loewenstein, & Thompson, 2003 ) and has been empirically connected to learning in multiple broadly conceived academic domains, including mathematics ( Alexander, White, & Daugherty, 1997 ); science ( Trey & Khan, 2008 ); reading ( Schiff & Ravid, 2007 ); and writing ( Holliway, 2007 )
Analogical thinking and its associated metastrategies may also be essential for the organization of memory and the development of language ( Hofstadter & Sander, 2013 )
An anomaly can be any occurrence or object that is abnormal or that digresses or deviates from an established pattern ( Ferguson & Sanford, 2008 ; Trickett, Trafton, & Schunn, 2009 )
The ability of students to strategically recognize or discern an anomaly has been tapped for over a century on tests of intelligence ( Binet, Simon, & Town, 1913 )
It has also been shown that attending to anomalies is critical for conceptual change in science ( Chinn & Malhotra, 2002 )

Some theorists argue that the process of anomaly resolution facilitates an individual’s understanding of his or her implicit assumptions and logical mistakes ( Darden, 1995 ), and that anomaly detection is the principal way in which scientific fields advance (T.S

Similar to analogical reasoning, students’ ability to employ metastrategies associated with attending to and reasoning with anomalies has been empirically linked to academic success in multiple academic domains, including mathematics ( Chen et al., 2007 ); science ( Trickett et al., 2009 ); and reading (Bohan & Sanford, 2008 )
Whenever a student strategically seeks to understand what something is by describing what it is not, the student is employing an antinomous metastrategy

This metastrategy can be particularly helpful in paradoxical situations in which a domain of study has come to accept two or more ideas that appear contradictory, when the issue of mutual exclusivity among categories, or the incompatibility of theoretical models is being reas oned with ( Chi & Roscoe, 2002 ; Opfer & Gelman, 2011 ; Sorensen, 2003 )

While the empirical study of students’ use of antinomous metastrategies remains largely underexplored (Dumas et al., 2012), the identification and consideration of antinomies have led to productive discussion and even discovery in a variety of academic disciplines,

Some scholars have argued that human language and thought are primarily organized through relations of opposition ( De Saussure, 1916/2011 ; Kjeldergaard & Higa, 1962 ; Marková, 1987 ), implying that antithetical metastrategies may have a deep-seated importance in human communication and cognition

The investigation of each of these four relational reasoning metastrategies—analogy, anomaly, antinomy, and antithesis—shows promise to be a potentially fruitful avenue of inquiry for those interested in students’ deeper processing of information and their subsequent building of principled knowledge

Because students’ ability to employ these metastrategies may be especially crucial in the modern information-saturated context (Dumas et al., 2013 ), we believe that the systematic examination of relational reasoning metastrategies—as well as how these metastrategies interface with more specific cognitive strategies and associated individual difference characteristics—will be an important addition to the larger literature on students’ strategic and metastrategic behavior

Strategies for Online Learning Another class of strategies that has entered into scholarly discourse in recent years is those strategies associated with learning on the Internet, including those involved in learning from hypertext ( Afflerbach & Cho, 2010 )
Hypertext can be defined as written text, pictures, video, or sound connected by electronic links ( Rasmussen, 2007 )
The collection of skills and strategies employed by learners in a hypertext environment has been referred to as “new-literacies” (e.g., Leu et al., 2008 )

As is implied by the use of this term, many scholars and researchers who either theoretically describe or empirically investigate this class of strategies conceptualize them as wholly novel and arising from the need for readers to interact with new technologies and texts (e.g., Coiro, 2003 )

However, while neither the observation that the sheer quantity of information available almost instantly via the Internet may present challenges and opportunities to students nor the assertion that readers’ strategies for dealing with this information and potentially deriving knowledge from it should be of interest to researchers are debated, significant questions remain about the characterization and classification of hypertext reading strategies

Afflerbach and Cho (2009) offered several specific examples of these strategies, including searching for relevant websites or information retrieval systems to access and overview possible target information; reducing the range of possible information to be encountered by generating keywords related to the topic and focus of a particular task; and scrutinizing Internet hypertextual links to anticipate and judge the usefulness and significance of the information before accessing it, based on specific reading goals; among others
However, these specific strategies could also be conceptualized as iterations of strategies that have long been used in traditional learning
Internet search strategies can be conceived as having an analog in traditional text searches
For instance, for as long as there have been collections of informational text (i.e., libraries), readers have needed to search various catalogs or organizational systems for information
These searches required the positing of keywords and the scrutiny of content summaries of various available texts before choosing one or more to read more deeply
While the technological platforms for these searches may change, their strategic function remains the same—to access the desired information in an efficient, effective way
In other words, new literacy strategies may not be Internet or hypertext specific but may have been employed in different technological contexts by generations of strategic learners
This debate is important not only for the theoretical conceptualization of hypertext reading strategies but also for the study and teaching of cognitive learning strategies at large
This is because the two competing conceptualizations of hypertext reading strategies make divergent implications for the fields of education and psychology

For example, if the strategies utilized by readers in a hypertext environment are wholly new and qualitatively different from those used when reading traditional text, then high- leverage strategies and metastrategies that have been perennially linked to student success—like the relational reasoning strategies described previously in this chapter— may not be able to be expected to translate to a hypertext environment
This would necessitate the teaching of hypertext-specific skills and strategies to students if they were to succeed in the twenty-first-century context

However, if, as we argue, the same skills and strategies that have undergirded success with traditional text (e.g., connecting to prior knowledge, making inferences about information not explicitly stated, questioning the author, relating aspects of the text to one another) will continue to be advantageously

Of course, we are not arguing that the specific instruction of computer or Internet skills is unimportant or should not be included in school curricula

Because these technologies are so ubiquitous today and a certain aptitude with them is likely required for any learner to succeed either in school or in the workplace, their use is certainly an important topic for instruction

In fact, because of the necessity of interacting with this technology, it is no surprise that investigations like that of Coiro (2011) have found significant effects of students’ online research ability to their hypertext reading comprehension
However, we do argue that the advent of hypertext does not, as Afflerbach and Cho (2010) have stated, represent a “change in the architecture of reading” (p
217), but rather it signifies a shift in the platform on which the act of reading is performed

This shift is likely to change the way cognitive strategies for reading manifest themselves and potentially alter the relative importance of certain strategies and skills, but, in our estimation, it will not fundamenta lly change the act of reading or the cognitive skills, strategies, or metastrategies required to be a successful reader now or in the future

Strategies in the Classroom In this chapter, we endeavor to show that students who are engaged in strategic behavior learn and perform better than students who are not strategic, and that strategic processing develops over time ( Bråten & Strømsø, 2003 ; Murphy & Alexander, 2002 ) and across domains and contexts ( Alexander & Judy, 1988 ; Butler, 1995 ; Murphy & Alexander, 2002 )
Being strategic requires that students have a repertoire of strategies and that they understand when and how to use them ( Slater & Horstman, 2002 )

Intervention research over the past 25 years has indicated that teachers have the potential to help their students learn strategies ( De La Paz, 2005 ; Jitendra et al., 2009 ; Keys, Hand, Prain, & Collins, 1999 ; Klinger, Vaughn, & Schumm, 1998 ;L.H
Yet, what challenges do teachers and students face in order for students to be good strategic processors, and what recommendations can be put forward to alleviate some of these challenges

Alexander and Judy (1988) stated, “It could be that schools perpetuate the accumulation of inert knowledge or reward routinized nonstrategic behavior” (p
While they did not elaborate much on this point, others have noticed a similar pattern

Writing around the same time as Alexander and Judy, Pressley, Goodchild, and colleagues (1989) addressed challenges to strategy instruction, emphasizing the importance of knowing when and where to use strategies

They also provided a list of suggestions for practitioners to address in order to aid students in their strategic processing, including recommendations to teach across-domain strategies and to motivate students to use the strategies they are taught

Building on the precedent for strategy instruction research set by Pressley and others (Duffy & Roehler, 1989 ; Swanson, 1989 ), Ruth Garner, in her 1990 article “When Children and Adults Do Not Use Learning Strategies: Toward a Theory of Settings,” explained why strategies are often not used within academic contexts

Garner put forward five reasons: poor cognitive monitoring, the use of primitive routines, knowledge deficiencies, goals that do not support strategic processing, and minimal transfer to novel situations
For students and teachers in the twenty-first century, these barriers may manifest differently, but we argue that these reasons continue to challenge strategic processing
First, Garner (1990) noted that strategic processing is hindered because students exhibit poor cognitive monitoring
She suggested that, “If children and adults do not notice that they are not learning, they are unlikely to seek a strategic remedy” (p
As is noted in research on metacognition, metacognitive strategies function to guide cognitive strategies, and the two are inextricably intertwined ( Flavell, 1979 )
If inefficient or ineffective metacognitive strategies are employed, then students may falsely believe that they understand the task when they may actually only grasp a portion of it ( Garner, 1990 )
In our estimation, systematic investigations aimed at improving students’ cognitive monitoring will not diminish in importance as the twenty-first century progresses

It takes place in a world where information is readily available in both print and digital formats ( Bohn & Short, 2009 ) and where using multiple devices and completing multiple tasks simultaneously is considered the norm ( Alexander & the DRLRL, 2012 ; Rideout, Foehr, & Roberts, 2010 )

Poor cognitive monitoring often results in surface-level rather than deep processing of vast information, preventing students from realizing that there is more to be learned from the content ( Garner, 1990 ), a particular concern for learners in the information age

Given these certain aspects of the modern technological context, the ability of students to monitor their own learning—as well as empirical investigations of that ability—will likely remain significant

For example, some summarizing routines encourage students to copy texts verbatim instead of requiring the reader to think deeply about the text and consider what information is important to keep or delete in the summary ( Garner, 1990 )
After using this summarizing routine, an effortless product is produced, but the routine prevents students from using strategies that would help them think more deeply about the text

However, students lack the ability to strategically synthesize information from multiple sources or evaluate the sources they encounter ( Metzger, Flanigan, & Zwarun, 2003 ; Walraven, Brand-Gruwel, & Boshuizen, 2009 )

Students’ maladaptive routines help them access the information online but do not help them make sense of the content or evaluate sources effectively ( Bråten, Strømsø, & Britt, 2009 ; List, Grossnickle, & Alexander, 2012 )
Third, Garner (1990) put knowledge deficiencies forward as another cause of students failing to use strategies

However, having a meager knowledge base also encompasses a lack of content-specific background knowledge ( Kaplan & Murphy, 2000 )
For example, a student cannot analyze the causes of the Civil War if the student does not understand the economic differences between the North and the South during the early 1860s
Additionally, a student cannot successfully learn long division if the student struggles with addition and subtraction
Because students today are surrounded by more information from multiple sources, they need to build expansive knowledge bases and use their background as a launch pad for strategic processing

Individuals are overloaded with information, yet fail to exhibit strategic behavior that would help them make sense of the information and engage in critical thinking
Fourth, Garner (1990) explained that classroom goals do not always support strategy use

Specifically, she indicated that classrooms tend to support either performance or mastery goal orientations, a finding that has been supported in recent literature ( Murayama & Elliot, 2009 ; Patrick, Kaplan, & Ryan, 2011 )

If students maintain a performance goal orientation (i.e., are motivated by demonstrating competence on outcomes relative to others; Ames & Archer, 1988 ), then they may not exhibit strategic activity, which requires effort and investment in the learning process ( Pressley, Goodchild, et al., 1989 )

Within the twenty-first-century context, classroom goals focus predominantly on acquiring high grades and doing well on standardized assessments ( Abrams, Pedulla, & Madaus, 2003 ; Guzenhauser, 2003 ; McNeil, 2000 )
Curricula focus on a breadth rather than a depth of knowledge; therefore, teachers reward students for simply regurgitating surface-level information
Students are not assessed on their strategic processing but instead are assessed on their ability to restate information or follow a heuristic when told to do so
Additionally, standardized tests are increasingly important as educational systems seek to link teacher pay to student test performance ( Springer & Gardner, 2010 ; Woessmann, 2011 )
As a result, teachers focus on techniques that will help students excel on a test instead of motivating students to learn complex content and develop thoughtful ideas about domain knowledge
Classroom conversations revolve around the ways to eliminate incorrect answer choices rather than analyzing arguments or developing opinions

The goal of school moves away from equipping students with essential knowledge and the ability to think strategically in new situations and instead emphasizes passing high-stakes assessments that require more rote processes than strategic processing ( Black & Wiliam, 1998 )
If teachers do not reward students for high-level thinking throughout the year, then they will not have an incentive to use strategies in the classroom
Finally, Garner (1990) explained that students exhibit minimal transfer of strategic activity to new situations
She noted: Teachers and researchers alike have observed an absence of generality of strategy use among students

Within the twenty-first-century context, students continue to struggle when encountering new situations
For example, a student might learn a questioning strategy to help comprehend the fictional novel Bridge to Terabithia by Katherine Paterson

However, the student may not realize that she can adjust this same questioning strategy and apply it when reading an article about global warming, solving a mathematics word problem, watching a video clip of Martin Luther King Jr.’s I Have a Dream speech, searching the Internet for information about current politicians, or engaging in social media websites
Today, students confront a variety of texts and problems, yet they often do not think strategically when encountering novel contexts
Despite these barriers to being strategic in a classroom, there are situations in which teachers and students can foster strategic thinking

We suggest that strategic thinking is promoted when (a) teachers and students understand what it means to be strategic, (b) teachers and students know how to apply strategies appropriate to the context, and (c) learner differences are considered
For strategy instruction to be effective, it is first necessary for teachers and students to understand what it means to be strategic

Researchers, practitioners, and students often lack clarity regarding the differences between strategies and skills, as well as differences between various types of strategies (Afflerbach et al., 2008 )
Teachers often mistake routinized skills for purposeful strategy use and subsequently focus on teaching skills instead of strategies
For students, this confusion may result in part from the frequent teaching of a series of steps to follow when attempting a particular task ( Bailin, Case, Coombs, & Daniels, 1999 )

For example, teachers might require students to follow the “sandwich model” of writing an essay, a model that provides students with a five-paragraph formula for writing an essay with an introduction, conclusion, and three supporting points

For example, teachers can broaden the categories they use when asking students to group mathematics problems ( Fuchs et al., 2003 )

Encouraging students to build a repertoire of strategies, to personalize and take ownership of those strategies, and to apply them adaptively when encountering novel situations aligns with the definition of strategies and supports students’ efforts to be strategic

In order for students to be able to pick strategies appropriate to the context, teachers and students should bundle strategies so that students do not use too many at once or one in isolation
Using a single strategy often does not provide students with the desired result of comprehending a text or discovering the solution to a difficult problem
Rather, a few strategies should be used in conjunction so that students can determine which strategies work best under what circumstances (Palincsar & Brown, 1984 )

The focus on bundling strategies emphasizes that not only may more than one strategy be appropriate in a given situation, but also helps students make sense of the strategies they are taught instead of becoming overwhelmed by too many options
For example, Palincsar and Brown (1984) taught summarizing, questioning, clarifying, and predicting strategies to seventh-grade students who were poor readers

When the strategies were taught together, learners’ reading comprehension improved, as demonstrated by both standardized and classroom comprehension assessments, and gains were maintained over time with the ability to utilize the strategies in new situations
As Palincsar and Brown (1984) suggested, students sometimes need to use multiple strategies simultaneously
However, students do not necessarily need all strategies ( Pressley & Afflerbach, 1995 ), so it is important to support students in determining which strategies help lead them to success.

The major contribution of Alexander and Judy’s (1988) article was to examine the interrelation between strategic processing and domain knowledge

Strategies do not act in isolation, rather they are initiated, enacted, and monitored by a learner who comes to any given situation with individual variation in knowledge as well as other factors, such as epistemic beliefs and motivation ( Richter & Schmid, 2010 ; Shen & Chen, 2006 ; Strømsø & Bråten, 2010 )

While Alexander and Judy’s focus was on domain knowledge and strategic processing, the consideration of interactions between strategies and individual differences more broadly is evident in the field today and provides a means by which learning settings can support strategy use

With regard to the interaction of knowledge and strategies, Alexander and Judy (1988) hypothesized domain knowledge is necessary for strategic processing, and that strategic processing is necessary for the use and acquisition of domain knowledge
Given the intervening years of empirical research supporting this hypothesis, learning environments should take students’ domain knowledge into account as a means of supporting strategic processing
Specifically, providing students with requisite domain knowledge or opportunities to access their prior knowledge before engaging with tasks requiring strategic processing is critical

As schools and standards move away from goals emphasizing the acquisition of domain knowledge toward goals emphasizing higher order thinking in the absence of knowledge goals (CCSS, 2010 ), the consideration of learner differences in domain knowledge and the importance of this reciprocal relation is often deemphasized, despite evidence of the central interaction

In addition to domain knowledge, students’ beliefs about the nature of knowledge (i.e., epistemic beliefs) have been examined more recently in relation to strategic processing (Bråten & Strømsø, 2006 ; Murphy & Mason, 2006 ; Sinatra & Pintrich, 2002 )

Understanding why an individual is successful or unsuccessful in implementing strategies is linked in important ways to a student’s epistemic beliefs, given that certain configurations of beliefs tend to be associated with more successful strategy use ( Muis & Franco, 2009 ; Strømsø & Bråten, 2010 )
Consideration of a student’s epistemic beliefs allows for an understanding of the knowledge related to the task from the lens of the student

If the student perceives knowledge about history to be simple and handed down from authority, this understanding would provide those within the learning setting the opportunity to scaffold the tasks provided for that student to guide the his or her understanding to include beliefs about the complexity of knowledge and the need for justification

Alexander and Judy (1988) briefly foreshadowed the recent surge of interest in motivation and strategic processing, noting that “motivational and social-contextual factors may impact the acquisition and utilization of domain-specific and strategic knowledge” (p
Although their review identified motivational factors as cursory variables in the studies they reviewed, interest in the motivation–strategy relation has expanded widely in
