Into the Future: What the Next 25 Years of Strategy Research Holds What we have sought to accomplish to this point in our examination of cognitive learning strategies was to revisit the groundbreaking article by Alexander and Judy (1988) and to ask whether the issues and concerns these researchers articulated years ago are as problematic or as pertinent today
Now, in this closing segment of the chapter we look ahead to the next 25 years
In effect, based on where we have come, what would we hold to be the future directions for theory and research on cognitive learning strategies

In preparing for this prospective look at cognitive learning strategies, we have decided to be bold and venturous in our prognostications, building on the trends that have begun to emerge within the contemporary literature and referenced herein

Specifically, we address four topics that we view as critical for continued progress in the area of cognitive learning strategies and that we hope will be richly explored in the years to come: (a) developmental and longitudinal investigations of strategy use; (b) neurophysiological indicators of strategic thinking and learning; (c) innovative measures and data-analytic procedures for the study of strategic processing in situ; and (d) academic environments constructed to promote strategic thinking and performance for all learners

Yet, even the impressive library of strategy-related research that now exists cannot serve to answer fundamental questions about how strategic processing—in conjunction with knowledge or motivation— should systematically change over the course of one’s academic development
Several years after the publication of Alexander and Judy’s 1988 article, Alexander (1997) theorized how such changes might unfold over time within academic domains

That is, what would the interplay of strategic processing, knowledge, and interest look like as individuals progress from the initial stage of learning (i.e., acclimation) into competence or even expertise
That theorizing took the form of the MDL (Alexander, 1997 , 2003 ), mentioned previously

However, while numerous studies of the MDL in a variety of academic domains have been undertaken (e.g., Kultural-Konak, Konak, Esparragosa, & Kremer, 2013 ; Langan & Athanasou, 2005 ; Schrader, Lawless, & Mayall, 2008 ), there remains no long-term, longitudinal examination of its viability

Yet, it is precisely such developmental and longitudinal investigations that are requisite to push understanding of the relation between cognitive strategies and academic development to the next level

Thus, should we return to this topic of cognitive strategies in 2038 or thereafter, we would hope to see a wealth of longitudinal investigations populating the literature and a more extensive understanding how strategic processing, in fact, develops over the life span

Neurophysiological Traces of Strategic Thinking Even though new technologies for the assessment of strategic processing are far more available today than in 1988 when Alexander and Judy wrote their article, the field of educational psychology still relies predominantly on self-report measures to chronicle strategic processing, be those measures real time, prospective, or retrospective in nature

However, if the increased presence of technologies like eye tracking or neurocognitive devices such as fMRI, ERP , and fNIRS, as well as their associated methodologies, continue to gain popularity as our previous discussion suggested, there is good reason to expect that the inclusion of neurophysiological indicators of strategic processing will be much more commonplace

Thus, in the literature on strategies published 25 years from now, researchers might be expected to do more than merely ask students to report what they strategically are planning to do (prospective), are doing (real time), or did (retrospective)
Whenever possible, researchers of the future might be called on to incorporate neurological or physiological data that can corroborate such self-reports

Advances in Measurement and Statistics Invariably, advancements in what can be learned in any complex arena are inextricably tied to the availability of measures and statistical procedures that allow for the gathering and interpreting of relevant data
In 1988, when Alexander and Judy first published their article, measures of strategic processing that were considered psychometrically sound were few and far between

It remains true today that measures of strategic processing are relatively limited in number and the psychometric properties of such measurement tools that often rely so heavily on self-report data or data pertaining to generic strategy use have increasingly been called in question (e.g., Samuelstuen & Bråten, 2007 )

Thus, for strategy research to reach the next level in the quarter century to come, it seems imperative that processing measures not only meaningfully reflect the domains or tasks at hand but also demonstrate that the resulting data meet acceptable psychometric standards

Similarly, such statistical procedures as structural equation modeling, multidimensional item-response theory (IRT), or mixture modeling were not commonly applied to the study of strategic processing—or any other educational construct for that matter—about 30 years ago
Those with the basic knowledge of these approaches were relatively few in number, and existing computer programs did not permit such procedures to be easily or quickly executed
Even if the programs did exist, computers of the time were simply not up to the task

Today, it is relatively easy to run many sophisticated statistical programs that were not even on the radar all those years ago, and many of today’s educational psychologists possess knowledge of a range of statistical procedures that would have seemed alien to their predecessors
Of course, how well they understand or appropriately apply those sophisticated statistical procedures is another matter entirely

Nonetheless, continuing our optimistic stance, we would hope that existing statistical tools continue to be refined and augmented so that conceptual and operational advancements in strategic processing and the multidimensional and dynamic natures of strategies can be duly assessed, modeled, and analyzed

Subscriber: OUP-Reference Gratis Access; date: 16 May 2018Since the 1970s, there has been the acknowledgment that strategies matter to human learning and development (e.g., Flavell, 1981 ; Garner, 1987 ) and that learners cannot be expected to demonstrate effective and efficient strategy use on a routine basis ( Garner, 1990 )
Thus, the need to remove barriers to strategic processing for students and to forge academic settings that promote strategic thinking and learning has continued unabated, as we strongly argued

Although the interest in cognitive strategies within the educational psychology literature has waxed and waned to a certain degree over the past 30 years, strategies will likely always have a place within the research community

Yet, much of the focus on enhancing strategic processing within educational settings over the past decades has targeted those students with special needs or identified learning difficulties (e.g., Fuchs et al., 2003 )
In effect, researchers engaged in classroom-based intervention in the realm of strategic processing have seen struggling learners and their teachers as their target audience

Looking forward to the year 2038, however, we would hope that research in strategic processing and academic development manifests a more encompassing view of the merits of devising facilitative learning environments

Armed with the knowledge garnered from developmental and longitudinal studies of strategic processing, prepared to gather both self-report and neurophysiological data, and informed by more precise measures and more sophisticated data-analytic tools, researchers over the next quarter century should seek to construct environments that meet the needs of diverse populations

Such settings must, by necessity, be flexible to the range of tasks and texts that learners encounter and sensitive to the individual differences of learners, including their own intentions and motivations for task engagement

In essence, it is hoped the days of one-size-fits-all strategic interventions will have passed into oblivion, giving way to more personalized and adaptable academic environments that grow and change as the needs of learners grow and change

Gone, as well, should be any notion that explicit attention to strategies is solely the purview of problem or struggling learners or that strategies need to be taught in isolation as an added component to existing curriculum

In the ideal academic setting, we are envisioning for 2043, cognitive learning strategies will be considered essential and integral aspects of the normal course of instruction for all subject matter domains and threaded naturally throughout that instruction whenever and wherever as the opportunity or need arises.

What intrigued us about that article were not only the principles about the relations between strategies and knowledge these authors derived from the literature but also the quandaries that remained for them and the field at that time

Across the years since the publication of that article, it is surprising how certain principles those authors forwarded are now simply accepted as “fact.” For instance, educational psychology researchers routinely acknowledge that the strategic behavior that should be evidenced in the performance of cognitive tasks will vary as a consequence of the knowledge learners possess about the domain and topic at hand

Likewise, the growing literature on conceptual change serves as substantial evidence to Alexander and Judy’s (1988) claim that “inaccurate or incomplete domain knowledge may inhibit or interfere with learning” (p
Just as surprising, areas of inquiry that were only beginning to appear on the horizon with regard to strategies have certainly come into full view over the decades
For instance, far greater understanding of the complex and intricate relation between learners’ strategic behaviors and their motivations (and emotions) has been achieved

The goals students’ espouse for their academic engagement ( Ames & Archer, 1988 ; Pintrich, 2000 ), the value or utility that they perceive for the task at hand ( Wigfield & Eccles, 2000 ), and their interest in or curiosity about the topics under study ( Ainley & Ainley, 2011 ; Hidi & Renninger, 2006 ) have all been shown to matter in the strategies students’ report or demonstrate and in the learning outcomes that result

Yet, for all that the field of educational psychology has come to understand about strategies over the past quarter century and more, many of the quandaries expressed by Alexander and Judy and others (e.g., Alexander et al., 1998 ; Garner, 1987 , 1990 ) remain
And, even more have come to light (e.g., Afflerbach & Cho, 2008 , 2010 ; Afflerbach et al., 2008 )

For instance, there is still limited understanding of how individuals’ strategic behaviors are influenced by their beliefs about knowledge and knowing (i.e., epistemic beliefs; Alexander & the DRLRL, 2012 ; King & Kitchener, 2002 )

There are also lingering questions about whether there are certain dispositional factors, such as a need for cognition or persistence ( Bråten, Ferguson, Anmarkrud, & Strømsø, 2013 ; Cacioppo & Petty, 1982 ; Petty, Briñol, Loersch, & McCaslin, 2009 ), or particular cognitive abilities such as rational or relational thinking ( Alexander & Baggetta, 2014 ; Stanovich, 2009 ; Stanovich, West, & Toplak, 2012 ) that increase the likelihood of effective strategic behavior
